title: SMTP Service Extension for Message Size Declaration
summary: Defines an SMTP extension that lets a client declare the size of a message in advance so the server can decline it, perhaps temporarily, before the whole thing is sent. It is an Internet Standard.

plainLanguage.summary: The SMTP SIZE extension lets a client tell the server how large a message is expected to be before sending its contents. The server can reject a message that exceeds its fixed limit or that it cannot currently store.

questions: what is the smtp size extension
how does smtp reject large messages early
how does smtp ehlo size work
subtitle: SMTP can check a message's declared size before the client sends its contents.

tldr.problem: Without a size declaration, an SMTP server may learn that it cannot store or accept a message only after the client has sent the entire message.
tldr.mechanism: The server advertises the SIZE extension in its EHLO response and may state a fixed maximum. The client can add a SIZE value to MAIL FROM so the server can accept or reject the estimated message size before DATA.
tldr.outcome: The extension can identify permanent size limits and temporary storage shortages before message transfer. RFC 1870 is an Internet Standard and obsoletes RFC 1653.

today: RFC 1870 is an Internet Standard and obsoletes RFC 1653. The unit metadata lists no RFC that updates or obsoletes it.

sections.title: Why Declare Message Size
sections.content:
MIME allows Internet mail to carry many kinds of data, increasing the range of message sizes an SMTP server may need to handle. A server has limited resources, including storage for incoming messages.

With unextended SMTP, the client may discover a size or storage failure only after sending the entire message, which the server then discards. If both sides support the size declaration extension, they can detect these conditions before starting the content transfer.
sections.plainLanguage: An SMTP server may not have enough room for a large message. SIZE lets the client provide an estimate before sending the message body.

sections.title: The SIZE Extension
sections.content:
The extension is announced with the SIZE keyword in the server's EHLO response. An optional decimal parameter gives the fixed maximum message size in bytes; a value of zero means there is no fixed maximum, while no parameter means the server has not stated a limit.

The extended MAIL FROM command can carry a SIZE parameter with the client's decimal estimate. Its value contains from 1 to 20 digits. The maximum MAIL FROM line length is increased by 26 characters to make room for the extension.

The extension adds no SMTP verbs. A client discovers support when an EHLO response with code 250 lists the SIZE keyword.
sections.plainLanguage: The server announces whether it supports SIZE and may give its fixed maximum message size. The client can then include an estimated size with MAIL FROM.

sections.title: What the Size Counts
sections.content:
Message size is the number of octets sent after the server replies 354 to DATA, including CR-LF pairs. It excludes the terminating dot and doubled quoting dots. The declared size is the client's estimate; the fixed maximum is the largest message the server will accept.

The estimate should include the headers, body and line-ending sequences. A client may use a heuristic when an exact count is impractical, and the RFC recommends choosing a method that usually overestimates. Only one SIZE parameter is allowed in a MAIL command.

A server must not use the SIZE parameter to determine where the DATA content ends. A server may accept a message that is somewhat larger than the declared size.
sections.plainLanguage: The size counts the message data and line endings, but not SMTP's ending dot or quoting dots. A client may estimate, but the estimate should usually be a little larger than the real message.

sections.title: Server and Client Responses
sections.content:
When the server receives MAIL FROM with SIZE, it can compare the estimate with its fixed maximum and check whether it has enough storage to accept the message. It may return 452 if storage is temporarily insufficient, or 552 if the message exceeds the fixed maximum.

After a 452 response, the client should reset or quit and try later. After a 552 response, it should stop that attempt and treat the message as undeliverable. A server may also return 452 or 552 for a particular recipient in response to RCPT.

A successful 250 response to MAIL FROM does not guarantee that the transfer will succeed. Clients must still handle errors after DATA or after the message has been sent, especially if their size estimate was too small.
sections.plainLanguage: A server can say it lacks storage for now or that the message is always too large. A positive answer before DATA does not guarantee later acceptance.

sections.title: Minimal Client and Server Use
sections.content:
A minimal client can compare its estimated message size with the fixed maximum advertised in EHLO and avoid sending messages the server will never accept. It does not need to use the extended MAIL command, but then it cannot learn about temporary storage limits or recipient-specific limits.

A minimal server can advertise a fixed maximum or no fixed maximum. It must accept the extended MAIL command and return 552 when a declared size exceeds its fixed limit. If it advertises SIZE without a maximum, it must check that it can store the declared message before returning 250 to extended MAIL.

The RFC's example has a server advertise a maximum of 1000000 bytes and a client declare 500000 bytes. The server accepts one recipient and refuses two others, one with 552 and one with 452.
sections.plainLanguage: A simple client can use the server's advertised maximum to avoid sending a message that is too large. A client that declares the size can also learn about temporary and recipient-specific limits.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC notes that size declarations could make a crude denial-of-service attack somewhat quicker or easier to arrange. It says the extension does not create a new vulnerability unless an implementation is particularly weak, since the underlying service already has these risks.

The document does not address trusted systems or possible information release through these mechanisms.
sections.plainLanguage: Publishing size limits could help an attacker make an existing SMTP denial-of-service attempt somewhat faster. The RFC says the extension does not create a new kind of vulnerability.
